# Security Rules — Java / Spring Boot + React

## SEC-001 — Secrets Management
- Always store secrets in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager. Never hardcode them in source code.
- Always add environment files to `.gitignore`. Never commit them.
- Never log a secret, a token or a connection string, even at debug level.
- Always inject secrets with `@Value("${property}")` or Spring Config Server. Never a literal in a `@Configuration` class.
- Always keep `application-local.properties` out of version control.

## SEC-002 — Authentication & Tokens
- Always store the access token in memory only. Never in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage`.
- Always store the refresh token in an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie.
- Always set short lifetimes: 15 minutes for the access token, 7 days for the refresh token.
- Always validate the token signature and the `exp`, `iss` and `aud` claims on every request.
- Never accept a token whose signing algorithm is read from the token itself.
- Always validate claims in the JWT filter before the request reaches a controller.

```java
// JWT filter: validate all claims
Claims claims = Jwts.parserBuilder()
    .setSigningKey(signingKey)
    .requireIssuer("taskflow-api")
    .requireAudience("taskflow-web")
    .build()
    .parseClaimsJws(token)
    .getBody();
```

## SEC-003 — Authorization & IDOR Prevention
- Always expose a `public_id` UUID in URLs and responses. Never expose the internal sequential identifier.
- Always apply least privilege: grant only the permissions the operation requires.
- Always verify that the resource belongs to the authenticated user's organization before returning or mutating it.
- Always read the tenant or organization identifier from the authenticated principal, never from the request payload.
- Always deny by default — a public endpoint is the exception and must be declared explicitly.
- Always enforce access at the method level with `@PreAuthorize`. Never rely on URL-only security.

```java
// Always verify org ownership, not just authentication
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER')")
public TaskResponse getTask(UUID taskUid, Long orgId) {
    return taskRepository.findByPublicIdAndOrgId(taskUid, orgId)
        .map(mapper::toResponse)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new TaskNotFoundException(taskUid));
}
```

## SEC-004 — Input Validation & Injection Prevention
- Always validate user input at the system boundary, before it reaches any business logic.
- Never pass user input to a shell command, a deserializer or a dynamic evaluation function.
- Always use parameterized queries. Never concatenate or interpolate user input into a query string.
- Always reject unknown fields instead of silently ignoring them.
- Always validate request bodies with Bean Validation (`@Valid`) on the controller parameter.
- Always use JPQL named parameters or `@Query` with `:param`.

```java
// Correct: parameterized JPQL
@Query("SELECT t FROM TaskEntity t WHERE t.title LIKE %:search% AND t.orgId = :orgId")
List<TaskEntity> searchByTitle(@Param("search") String search, @Param("orgId") Long orgId);

// Forbidden: string concatenation
// "SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE title LIKE '%" + userInput + "%'"
```

## SEC-005 — Output Encoding & XSS Prevention
- Always rely on the framework's default output escaping.
- Always sanitize HTML with a vetted library before injecting it, and prefer not injecting raw HTML at all.
- Always set `Content-Type: application/json` explicitly on API responses, and never return HTML from an API endpoint.
- Always render through JSX, which escapes by default, rather than `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
- Always configure the response headers through Spring Security.

## SEC-006 — CORS
- Always whitelist explicit origins. Never use a wildcard origin in production.
- Always restrict the allowed methods to those the API actually serves.
- Always enable credentialed requests only when cookies are required, and only together with explicit origins.
- Always declare the policy in a `CorsConfigurationSource` bean rather than per-controller annotations.

```java
@Bean
CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
    CorsConfiguration config = new CorsConfiguration();
    config.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://taskflow.app"));
    config.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"));
    config.setAllowCredentials(true);
    return new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
}
```

## SEC-007 — CSRF
- Always enable CSRF protection on any endpoint a browser can reach with a cookie-based session.
- A stateless API may skip CSRF only when no cookie takes part in authentication.
- Always set `SameSite=Strict` on the refresh token cookie as defence in depth.
- Always keep Spring Security's CSRF filter enabled when a session or refresh cookie is used.

## SEC-008 — Logging & Error Exposure
- Always log security events: failed logins, rejected tokens, authorization failures.
- Always exclude PII from logs: emails, names, phone numbers, addresses, tokens, passwords.
- Always return a generic message to the client and keep the diagnostic detail in the server log.
- Never expose a stack trace, a query or an internal identifier in an API response.
- Always map exceptions in a `@RestControllerAdvice` so no handler leaks an internal message.

```java
// Correct: generic message to client, details in server log
log.warn("Authentication failed for user: {} — {}", maskedEmail, reason);
throw new BadCredentialsException("Invalid credentials");

// Forbidden: exposing internals
throw new BadCredentialsException("User john@example.com not found in database");
```

## SEC-009 — Dependency Security
- Always pin dependency versions. Avoid open ranges in production builds.
- Always commit the lockfile so the audited tree is the deployed tree.
- Always review the changelog, the licence and the maintenance status before adding a dependency.
- Always update dependencies in a dedicated `chore(deps):` change, never mixed with feature work.
- Always run `mvn dependency-check:check` and `npm audit` before a release.

## SEC-010 — Cryptography
- Always use a cryptographically secure random source for tokens, nonces and identifiers. Never a general-purpose random function.
- Never design a cryptographic scheme. Use the platform primitives.
- Always hash passwords with BCrypt at strength 12 or above. Never MD5, SHA-1 or a plain SHA-256.
- Always generate tokens with `java.security.SecureRandom`.

## SEC-011 — Security Headers
- Always send `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
- Always send a `Content-Security-Policy` that defaults to `'self'`.
- Always send `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` or stricter.
- Always set the headers centrally, never per endpoint.
- Always configure the headers through Spring Security's `headers()` DSL.

```java
http.headers(headers -> headers
    .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives("default-src 'self'"))
    .frameOptions(frame -> frame.deny())
    .xssProtection(xss -> xss.enable())
    .referrerPolicy(referrer -> referrer.policy(ReferrerPolicyHeaderWriter.ReferrerPolicy.STRICT_ORIGIN))
);
```

## SEC-012 — HTTPS & Transport Security
- Always serve production traffic over HTTPS only, and redirect plain HTTP.
- Always send `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` in production.
- Always require TLS 1.2 as a minimum and disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1.
- Always mark every cookie `Secure` in production.
- Always enforce the channel with `requiresSecure()` rather than relying on the proxy alone.
